questions.question: Define tokens and their use in programming.
questions.answer: A token is the smallest meaningful lexical unit of source code recognized by the compiler. C token categories include keywords (int), identifiers (count), constants (10), string literals ("Hello"), operators (+, <=), and punctuation/separators (;, parentheses, braces). Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens before syntax analysis.

questions.question: Differentiate low-level and high-level languages.
questions.answer: Low-level languages (machine/assembly) are close to hardware, often architecture-specific, and require detailed control of registers/addresses; execution is efficient but development is harder. High-level languages (C, Python, Java) offer abstractions, readable syntax and typically better portability, but require a compiler/interpreter and still vary in performance. C combines high-level constructs with low-level capabilities.

questions.question: Significance of operators in programming languages.
questions.answer: Operators express calculations, comparisons, assignment, logic and bit manipulation. C examples: arithmetic +,-,*,/,%; relational <,<=,==,!=; logical &&,||,!; assignment =,+=; increment ++; bitwise &,|,^,<<,>>; conditional ?:; address-of & and dereference *. Precedence/associativity determine grouping; parentheses clarify intent.

questions.question: State time complexity of selection sort.
questions.answer: Selection sort finds the minimum among the remaining items in each pass. Comparisons: (n−1)+(n−2)+…+1=n(n−1)/2, so best/average/worst-case time is Θ(n²); swaps O(n); auxiliary space Θ(1) for in-place version.

questions.question: Define macros and their use in C.
questions.answer: A macro is a preprocessor text substitution defined with #define. Examples: #define LIMIT 100 and #define SQUARE(x) ((x)*(x)). Uses: compile-time constants, conditional compilation, simple generic substitutions. Macros are not type-checked and may evaluate arguments more than once; prefer const, enum or inline functions when appropriate.

questions.question: Define object file and describe compilation process in C.
questions.answer: An object file (.o/.obj) contains machine code and metadata (symbols, relocation entries) produced from a translation unit, usually not yet a complete executable. Stages: (1) preprocess headers/macros (#include/#define), (2) compile tokens/parsing/type checks/optimizations into assembly or internal IR, (3) assemble into relocatable object file, (4) link object files and libraries resolving external references, (5) loader maps executable into memory at runtime. GCC demo: gcc -E hello.c -o hello.i; gcc -S hello.c -o hello.s; gcc -c hello.c -o hello.o; gcc hello.o -o hello.

Explain the use and importance of linked lists in programming.
questions.answer: A linked list is a dynamic collection of nodes, each storing a value and a link to its successor (and optionally predecessor). Nodes need not be contiguous. Benefits: dynamic growth and O(1) insertion/deletion when node/preceding pointer known; useful for adjacency lists, chained hashes, queues and polynomial terms. Drawbacks: extra pointer memory, O(n) indexed access and poor cache locality. Types: singly, doubly and circular linked lists.

questions.question: Draw and discuss digital computer system architecture and use in programming.
questions.answer:
Logical organization:
Input devices → I/O controller ↔ System bus ↔ CPU (control unit + ALU + registers)
                                      ↕
                                Main memory (RAM)
                                      ↕
                              Secondary storage
The control unit fetches/decodes instructions; ALU performs arithmetic and logic; registers store immediate operands/state; memory stores code/data; I/O controllers connect devices, and buses carry addresses/data/control. A program is compiled/loaded into memory, CPU executes the instruction cycle, and the OS mediates devices and storage. Registers and cache provide faster access than RAM, which is faster than disk.

questions.question: List the four storage classes in C with examples.
questions.answer:
Classic C storage-class specifiers taught here: auto, register, static, extern.
auto int x=5; // block-local automatic lifetime (auto normally implicit).
register int i; // hints fast access; address-of on such an object is not allowed in standard C.
static int calls=0; // static-duration local retains its value between calls; file-scope static restricts linkage.
extern int total; // declares variable defined elsewhere with external linkage.
Lifetime, scope and linkage are distinct concepts; storage-class keywords influence these properties.

questions.question: Explain different operators in C with examples.
questions.answer: Arithmetic + - * / % (7/2=3 for integer division); relational < <= > >= == != (producing 0/1); logical && || ! (short-circuit for &&/||); assignment = += -= *= /=; ++/--; bitwise & | ^ ~ << >> on integers; conditional expression condition ? yes : no; sizeof; pointer/address operators * and &; indexing []; member access . and ->. Operators have precedence/associativity; use parentheses for clear expressions.
